# Pilot claim re-check: results

2026.10.04 · Mr. Radio, for Rick · companion to the documentation rewrite plan (plan 1 of 2), Phase 3 step 1, store item `18c8a3b2`

This page reports one run of the claim harness over the pilot rewrite of the five `task_store_*.py` modules. The harness reads each of the 78 docstrings in its original form, lists the claims it makes, and asks a judge whether each claim is still stated in the rewritten form. A claim the judge cannot find is called missing.

The run compares the original text (commit `ced08ca19`) with the rewrite pinned as `refs/keep/maya-pilot-restore` (commit `7f5c619de`), called the restored rewrite on this page. The first rewrite (commit `7f1f4dc41`) was checked the same way on 2026-10-02 by Maya, and her figures are set beside these.

## 1. What the run shows

1. **The restored rewrite loses fewer claims.** 48 of 78 docstrings have a claim judged missing, against 55 for the first rewrite. Distinct missing claims fell from 523 to 300.
2. **The claims both extractor lists agree on fell further.** 83 claims are judged missing in both lists, against 215.
3. **The worst docstrings improved most.** Eight docstrings lost more than 20 claims in the first rewrite. One does now.
4. **Two thirds of the missing claims sit in 14 docstrings.** Those 14 hold 199 of the 300.
5. **55 of the 300 are tagged as history.** The tag marks a claim that carries a date, an incident or a row id. It is an aid to the readers and excuses nothing.
6. **Two readers then sorted the 300, each alone.** Both call 2 claims real losses, 10 moved to a neighbouring docstring, and the other 288 history or judge error. Section 9 has the sort, section 10 the cost and time, section 11 the whole pilot in one table.

## 7. What this run does not say

1. **Whether any missing claim is a real loss.** The judge says a claim is absent. The pass rule on store item `18c8a3b2` is that two readers, each alone, sort every absent claim into history, judge error, real loss or unsure, and the pilot passes on zero real loss and zero unsure. Section 9 reports that sorting, done after sections 1 to 8 were written.
2. **Whether the gate passed.** The report prints `default_gate_pass=False`. Maya's run of the first rewrite printed the same and she attributed it to the pairs carrying no seeded removal. The cause was not checked for this run.
3. **How much the extractor misses.** A claim the extractor never lists cannot be judged missing. This run does not measure that.
4. **How much of the fall is the text and how much is the draw.** Each rewrite was checked once, with one draw of the two extractor lists. The two runs also differ in pairs file, harness tree and CLI version. The prompt versions are the same.

Tiberius and Sam each sorted all 300 claims alone on 2026-10-04, from a numbered worksheet and the full old and new text of the 48 docstrings. Neither saw the other's file. Classes: history (a date, an incident, a row id, who decided what), judge error (the claim is still stated in the same docstring, with the words quoted), real loss, unsure. A fifth class, moved, was added in the second round: the fact is stated in a different docstring of the five modules, named and quoted.

### How the sort was checked

Every judge error note had to quote the new text. A script looked for each quote in the docstring's new text. The first pass failed that check on 33 of Sam's 164 notes and 25 of Tiberius's 168. Both readers re-read those claims. Sam changed the class of 11; Tiberius rewrote 29 notes with exact quotes. The moved class came out of that round: several quotes were exact, in a different docstring.

Pass rule on store item `18c8a3b2` (Cheech, written before the run): zero real loss and zero unsure. **By that rule the pilot does not pass as it stands: 2 real losses.** Rick ruled on 2026-10-03 that the pilot has no measured gate on claim loss and that he decides from the full summary.

Limits: both readers are Sonnet seats, the same model family that wrote the rewrite. The first pass took each reader under six minutes for 300 claims, and the quote check then overturned or corrected about one judge error note in six. The readers saw each other's notes on 12 claims in the second round, so those 12 are not independent. The 143 claims both call judge error were not read by a third party.

## 10. Cost and time

Every model call in the pilot ran under the Max plan, so no per-token money was spent. The cost is time and plan usage.

| Step | Pilot: 78 docstrings, 19,448 words of old text | Whole production pool: 6,070 docstrings, 471,973 words |
|---|---|---|
| Docstring length | mean 249 words, median 174 | mean 78 words, median 51 |
| Writer, first rewrite | 795 seconds of agent time, 17.0 minutes per 100 docstrings (Maya, 2026-10-02) | about 5.4 hours, scaled by words |
| Writer, restore pass (`7f5c619de`) | not recorded | unknown |
| Claim check, wall time | 275 minutes over two legs, 699 model calls, one docstring at a time | about 111 hours scaled by words, 356 hours scaled by docstring count |
| Two-reader sort | 31 minutes from spawn to both final files, of which 10 were a message of mine that did not arrive | not projected |

The pool figures are from `labelled-set-2026.10.03/pool/pool.jsonl` at commit `dae3f14d1`, which leaves out the 78 pilot docstrings.

The projection is from one run. The pilot docstrings are three times the average length, so scaling by words is the fairer of the two figures. Either way the claim check as built is too slow to run one docstring at a time over every package in a one-train-a-day sweep. It would need to run several docstrings at once, or over a sample of each package.

## 12. Accuracy, cost, and a faster method

Rick asked four things on reading sections 1 to 11: how accurate the rewrite is, what rewriting costs in time and tokens, how to cut the 111 hours, and what the best method looks like. One correction first: **the 111 hours is the claim check, not the rewriting.** The writer is fast. The check is slow, and 91% of its time is the judge model's hidden thinking.

### 12.1 Accuracy

| Measure | Figure | Read it as |
|---|---|---|
| Real losses in the restored rewrite | 2 claims, of about 1,354 the extractor lists per run | about 0.15% of claims lost; 95% upper bound about 0.5% |
| Docstrings with no real loss | 76 of 78 | 97% |
| Real losses in the first rewrite, before any check | 261 put back by the restore commit, 23 more unsure, of 523 flagged | between one claim in five and one in ten lost by a single writing pass |
| Contract lines (Requires, Ensures) | 0 lost of 6 flagged; 1 weakened of 34 changed | repaired in `3da2dd2ec` |
| Reader test | 58 of 78 answers right before, 61 after | no worse |
| The judge's "missing" verdicts that the readers uphold | 2 real loss + 10 moved + about 125 history, of 300 | about half of the judge's alarms are wrong: the claim is still there |

The low loss figure is the product of the whole loop: write, check, read the alarms, restore. A single writing pass lost between one claim in five and one in ten. The first row counts losses among claims the extractor listed; a claim it never lists is not counted, and that share is not measured.

The range comes from dividing the 261 restored claims by one extractor list (about 1,345 claims, one in five) and by both lists together (2,690, one in ten). The 261 were counted across both lists, and how far the two lists overlap was not measured.

### 12.2 What the pilot cost

All calls ran under the Max plan, so the money cost per token is zero. Tokens below are read from the session transcripts of both legs of the claim check, each model message counted once.

| Step | Time | Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Writer, first rewrite (4 Sonnet workers) | 795 seconds of agent time | not recorded; the output is about 13,400 words, so tens of thousands of output tokens |
| Writer, restore pass | not recorded | not recorded |
| Claim check: Sonnet extractor, 223 calls | 22.5 minutes (8%) | 331,000 in, 217,000 out |
| Claim check: Haiku judge, 468 calls | 242.5 minutes (91%) | 736,000 in, 1,848,000 out |
| Claim check: Opus on split votes, 8 calls | 0.3 minutes | 11,000 in, 1,600 out |
| Claim check, total | 275 minutes wall, 265 inside model calls | 1.08 million in, 2.07 million out |
| Two readers sorting 300 alarms | 31 minutes wall | not recorded |

The judge spends 3,949 output tokens per call on average, against 972 for the extractor. Its visible answer is a short JSON list of about 200 tokens. The rest is extended thinking, which the Claude command-line tool turns on for Haiku by default: every judge session read holds a thinking block, and the visible text is 5% of the output tokens. The Sonnet extractor's sessions hold none. An earlier version of this section said the judge was writing long answers; that was the wrong cause.

| | Docstrings | Words |
|---|---|---|
| All production docstrings in those files | 6,228 | 476,848 |
| No lint finding: nothing to rewrite | 3,751 (60%) | 149,713 (31%) |
| 1 finding | 772 | |
| 2 to 5 findings | 842 | |

Of 20,452 findings, 13,217 (65%) are one rule: a word in capitals used as emphasis. Lowering the case of a word changes no claim.

### 12.4 Where the 111 hours goes, and what cuts it

| Change | Effect on the claim check | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Check only docstrings the writer changed | 111 hours to about 77 | 60% of docstrings have no finding and hold 31% of the words | none: unchanged text cannot lose a claim |
| Fix capitals by script, not by the writer | fewer docstrings rewritten at all | 65% of findings | low; needs a list of real acronyms |
| Turn off the judge's thinking | measured: a judge call takes 2.9 seconds, not 31.1 | section 12.6 | it let through 8 history claims the thinking judge caught; its miss rate must be measured on the labelled gate set |
| One judge run, Opus only on "missing" | judge calls cut to a third | the three runs agree on 92% of claims | fewer second opinions on "present"; same measurement needed |
| One extractor list | extractor calls halved | both real losses were found by both lists | weak: two losses is a small sample |
| Run 8 docstrings at once | wall time cut by 8 | the harness runs one at a time by design | Max plan rolling window; needs a rate check |
| Judge against the whole file, not one docstring | removes the "moved" alarms | 10 of 300 alarms were facts that moved next door | none found |

With the third and fourth changes measured (section 12.6), the pilot's check is 22.5 minutes of extractor plus 7.8 of judge, about 30 minutes against 275. Scaled by words that is about 12 hours of serial time for the whole code base, about 8.5 hours for the changed docstrings only, and about an hour at 8 wide. The whole-code-base figures are still projections from the pilot. The extractor is now three quarters of the time, so one extractor list is the next cut.

### 12.5 The method this points to

1. **Select.** Lint every package. Docstrings with no finding are left alone.
2. **Mechanical fixes first.** Capitals, glyphs and bare references that a script can fix go through a script, with the docs-only check proving no code changed.
3. **Write once, with the restore rules in the prompt.** The first pass lost reasons because the prompt did not say to keep them. The restore pass's rule ("history may go; reasons and behaviours stay, as present-tense properties") belongs in the writer's prompt, so the second pass is not needed. This is the step the pilot has not tested.
4. **Deterministic checks.** Docs-only diff, contract diff, lint. Seconds per package.
5. **Claim check, slimmed.** One extractor list, one judge run with thinking off against the whole file's new text, Opus on each "missing", 8 docstrings at once. Only on docstrings the writer changed.
6. **One reader, with a quote check.** The reader sorts only the alarms, and every "still stated" verdict must quote the new text or it is sent back. Two readers agreed on the loss count here; the quote check, not the second reader, is what caught the errors.
7. **Restore and merge per package** on a green unit tier.

Two things are owed before the sweep runs this way. The thinking-off judge's miss rate must be measured on the labelled gate set, where the removed claims are known. And thinking must become a setting of the model call in `model_transport.py`, which is a code change for an author and a reviewer; section 12.6 used a throwaway rig.

### 12.6 The judge with thinking off, measured

Run 2026-10-04, 13:51 to 13:59 EDT. The judge stage only, over all 78 pilot docstrings, with the extractor's claim lists reused from the full run so the claims are identical. One judge run per list in place of three, Haiku's thinking disabled, the same prompt, Opus still asked on "uncertain". A throwaway rig outside the repository; no code changed.

| | Full run: thinking on, three runs | Thinking off, one run |
|---|---|---|
| Haiku judge calls | 468 | 156 |
| Seconds per judge call, mean | 31.1 | 2.9 |
| Judge stage, total | 242.5 minutes | 7.8 minutes |
| Judge output tokens | 1,848,000 | 41,000 |
| Output tokens per call | 3,949 | 265 |
| Thinking blocks in the sessions | one in every session read | none |
| Opus calls | 8 | 6 |
| Distinct claims called missing | 300 | 220 |

| What the two readers called the claim | In the full run's 300 | Also raised with thinking off |
|---|---|---|
| Real loss | 2 | 2 |
| Moved to another docstring | 10 | 8 |
| History, both readers | 121 | 113 |
| Judge error, both readers | 143 | 47 |
| History or judge error, readers differ | 24 | 20 |

It raised both real losses, in both extractor lists. It dropped 96 of the 143 alarms the readers call judge errors, so a reader has less noise to sort. It also raised 30 claims the full run did not; nobody has read those.

The cost shows in the history row: 8 claims that both readers agree are absent from the new text were called present. None of the 8 is a loss, but a judge that calls an absent claim present can miss a real loss the same way. Two real losses is too small a sample to put a number on that. The labelled gate set exists to measure it.
